steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on the rotational stability of soft fingers in precision grasps, motivating a model of rotational stability and stating our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Soft fingers: strengths in enclosing grasps
- Limited force capacity, especially for precision grasps
- Existing mechanical design approaches vs grip parameters
- Observed rotational instability
- Grip stability and slip models and their gaps
- Our approach and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Strengths
  - soft fingers grasp sensitive objects, handle geometry variation; spherical/cylindrical objects -> enclosing grasp
  - enclosing/power grasp: large contact area, good for pick-and-place in unobstructed environments
- Limits
  - reduced force capacity vs rigid fingers; limits payload and contact-rich tasks
  - worse with reduced contact area: smaller or flat objects, precision grasp (fingertip, pinch) e.g. dexterous manipulation in clutter
  - 3+ fingers help, but small, non-round, cluttered objects often need two-finger parallel grasp
- Mechanical design
  - stiffening elements, jamming, incompressible actuating fluids, additional kinematic structure, structured compliance
  - force capacity also affected by grip parameters: degree of actuation, robot grip pose, finger distance
- Rotational instability
  - range of fingers and objects (Fig. 1 (a)); pressure increase -> object rotates, sometimes slip (Fig. 1 (b))
  - limits raising force capacity via pressure; affected by grasp parameters
  - tuning grip parameters relies on user experience or computational simulation
- Grip stability and slip
  - grip stability: wide range of definitions; planar: force-closure, form-closure, stiff-but-underactuated fingers
  - assume point, infinitely stiff contact -> unrealistic for soft fingers
  - finger compliance modelled for tendon-driven fingers, spherical fingertips; soft fingers rotate (Figure 1, video) -> need bulk motion model
  - slip: Coulomb friction, point-contact model; questionable with larger contact area
  - friction models for spherical soft fingertips proposed, not validated on general soft fingers
- This paper
  - model for rotational stability; validate bulk Coulomb model
  - effect of contact area, pressure, offset -> increasing normal force is primary way; but can cause dynamic instability
  - rotational instability modelled with linear finger stiffness; rotational stability vs classical grip stability
  - validated on range of objects, grip conditions, soft fingers (PneuNet and commercial); use model to find grip parameters
- Contributions
  - 1. analytical model relating rotation angle to bulk stiffness
  - 2. empirical relationship between grasp parameters and model variables; validate coulomb friction; effects on bulk stiffness
  - 3. validation comparing force/angle prediction vs actual; simple case optimizing grasping parameters

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Soft fingers can grasp sensitive objects and handle geometry variation, especially with spherical or cylindrical objects where you can use an enclosing grasp. An enclosing or power grasp gives a large contact area between the finger and the object, and it is well-suited to pick-and-place tasks in unobstructed environments.

But soft fingers usually have reduced force capacity compared with rigid fingers, which limits payload and contact-rich tasks. This limitation matters a lot when the contact area is reduced: when smaller or flat objects are grasped, or when a precision grasp like a fingertip or pinch grasp is needed, e.g. to manipulate dexterously in cluttered environments. Three or more fingers can be used to improve the grasp, but objects that are smaller, not round, or in cluttered environments often need a parallel grasp with two fingers.

Ongoing work explored increasing grasp strength through mechanical design, using stiffening elements, jamming techniques, incompressible actuating fluids, additional kinematic structure, and structured compliance. Mechanical design is important, but the force capacity is also affected by grip parameters like degree of actuation, robot grip pose, and finger distance.

- grasping instability on range of fingers and objects (Fig. 1 (a)); more pressure -> rotation, sometimes slip (Fig. 1 (b)); limits force capacity; tuning grip parameters by experience or simulation
- grip stability definitions; force-closure, form-closure, stiff-but-underactuated; point + infinitely stiff contact unrealistic; compliance models for tendon-driven fingers, spherical fingertips; need bulk motion
- slip: Coulomb point-contact model; spherical fingertip friction models not validated on general soft fingers
- this paper: rotational stability model, bulk Coulomb model; contact area, pressure, offset; normal force; linear finger stiffness; validated on PneuNet and commercial fingers
- contributions 1-3

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Soft fingers can grasp sensitive objects and handle geometry variation, especially with spherical or cylindrical objects where you can use an enclosing grasp. An enclosing or power grasp gives a large contact area between the finger and the object, and it is well-suited to pick-and-place tasks in unobstructed environments.

But soft fingers usually have reduced force capacity compared with rigid fingers, which limits payload and contact-rich tasks. This limitation matters a lot when the contact area is reduced: when smaller or flat objects are grasped, or when a precision grasp like a fingertip or pinch grasp is needed, e.g. to manipulate dexterously in cluttered environments. Three or more fingers can be used to improve the grasp, but objects that are smaller, not round, or in cluttered environments often need a parallel grasp with two fingers.

Ongoing work explored increasing grasp strength through mechanical design, using stiffening elements, jamming techniques, incompressible actuating fluids, additional kinematic structure, and structured compliance. Mechanical design is important, but the force capacity is also affected by grip parameters like degree of actuation, robot grip pose, and finger distance.

Grasping instability can be seen on a range of fingers and objects in Fig. 1 (a). When the pressure increases, as seen in Fig. 1 (b), the object starts to rotate, and sometimes this leads to slip at the contact with the fingers. We observe that this rotational instability limits how much force capacity can be increased by increasing pressure, and that it is affected by grasp parameters. Because soft fingers are complex, tuning these grip parameters often relies on the experience of the users or on computational simulation.

This rotational instability is influenced by both grip stability and slip. Grip stability has many definitions. Planar grip stability was studied for force-closure, form-closure, and stiff-but-underactuated fingers. But these analyses assume that the contact is a point and infinitely stiff, so they are unrealistic for soft fingers. Some approaches do model finger compliance for tendon-driven fingers or spherical fingertips. However, soft fingers can have rotational instability, as seen in Figure 1 and the attached video, and this requires modelling the bulk motion of the fingers.

In grasping, slip is usually modelled with Coulomb friction. But a Coulomb friction model is a point-contact model, so it is not clear whether it applies when soft fingers have a larger contact area. Friction models for spherical soft fingertips were proposed, but they were not validated on general soft fingers.

To increase the force capacity of soft fingers, this paper proposes a model for rotational stability and validates the bulk Coulomb model. Compared with friction modelling in soft fingers, we look at the effect of contact area, pressure, and offset. This suggests that increasing normal force is the main way to increase force capacity. But increasing normal force can lead to dynamic instability. Rotational instability is modelled with linear finger stiffness. Compared with classical grip stability, this is the rotational stability. We validate these models experimentally on a range of objects, grip conditions, and soft fingers (PneuNet and commercial fingers). Then we use the model to find grip parameters that improve force capacity.

To sum up, our contributions are: 1. an analytical model of rotational stability in soft finger’s precision grasping that relates rotation angle to bulk stiffness; 2. finding empirically the relationship between grasp parameters and the model variables, validating coulomb friction and finding the effects on bulk stiffness; 3. validating the model by comparing the force/angle of the model prediction and the actual results, and introducing a simple case that uses the model to optimize the grasping parameters.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Soft fingers can grasp sensitive objects and handle geometry variation, especially with spherical or cylindrical objects where an enclosing grasp can be used [1,2]. An enclosing or power grasp gives a large contact area between finger and object, and is well-suited to pick-and-place tasks in unobstructed environments [3].

However, soft fingers typically have reduced force capacity compared with rigid fingers [4,5], limiting payload [6] and contact-rich tasks [7]. This limitation is significant when the contact area is reduced: when smaller or flat objects are grasped, or when a precision grasp, such as a fingertip or pinch grasp, is needed, e.g. to manipulate dexterously in cluttered environments [8]. Although three or more fingers can be used to improve the grasp, objects which are smaller, not round, or in cluttered environments often require a parallel grasp with two fingers.

Ongoing work has explored increasing grasp strength through mechanical design: using stiffening elements [9], jamming techniques [10], incompressible actuating fluids [6], additional kinematic structure [11], and structured compliance [12]. While mechanical design is important, the force capacity is also affected by grip parameters such as degree of actuation, robot grip pose, and finger distance.

Grasping instability can be seen on a range of fingers and objects in Fig. 1 (a). When pressure increases, as seen in Fig. 1 (b), the object begins to rotate, sometimes leading to slip at the contact with the fingers. We observe that this rotational instability limits the ability to increase force capacity by increasing pressure, and that it is affected by grasp parameters. Due to the complexity of soft fingers, tuning these grip parameters often relies on the experience of the users or on computational simulation [13].

This rotational instability is influenced by both grip stability and slip. Grip stability has a wide range of definitions [14,15]. Planar grip stability has been studied for force-closure [16], form-closure [17], and stiff-but-underactuated fingers [18]. However, these analyses assume the contact is a point and infinitely stiff, making them unrealistic for soft fingers. Some approaches do model finger compliance [15] for tendon-driven fingers [19] or spherical fingertips [20]. However, soft fingers can have rotational instability [8], as seen in Figure 1 and the attached video, which requires modelling the bulk motion of the fingers.

Slip is typically modelled with Coulomb friction in grasping [14,21]. However, a Coulomb friction model is a point-contact model, raising questions about its applicability to the larger contact area of soft fingers. Friction models for spherical soft fingertips have been proposed [22,23,20], but have not been validated on general soft fingers.

Towards increasing the force capacity of soft fingers, this paper proposes a model for rotational stability and validates the bulk Coulomb model. Compared with friction modelling in soft fingers [21,23], we examine the effect of contact area, pressure, and offset. This suggests that increasing normal force is the primary way to increase force capacity. However, increasing normal force can lead to dynamic instability. Rotational instability is modelled considering linear finger stiffness. Compared with classical grip stability [14,16,17,18,19], this is rotational stability. These models are validated experimentally on a range of objects, grip conditions, and soft fingers (PneuNet [24] and commercial fingers). We then use the model to find grip parameters which improve force capacity.

In summary, we make the following contributions: 1. an analytical model of rotational stability in soft finger’s precision grasping relating rotation angle to bulk stiffness; 2. empirically finding the relationship between grasp parameters and the model variables, validating coulomb friction and finding the effects on bulk stiffness; 3. validating the model by comparing the force/angle between the model prediction and actual results, and introducing a simple case using the model to optimize the grasping parameters.
